slides.0.title: Nova Scotia
slides.0.subtitle: The Annapolis Valley and Tidal Bay: L'Acadie Blanc in a maritime climate
slides.1.title: History and regions
slides.1.highlights.0.title: From the 1600s to 1979
slides.1.highlights.0.content: In 1634 Acadia's governor Isaac de Razilly wrote that Bordeaux vines planted at La Hève were "doing very well"; the Kentville Research Station began variety trials in 1913; commercial production dates from 1979 when Grand Pré Winery opened; the Wine Association of Nova Scotia (WANS) was created in 2003 (Wikipedia)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Four main regions
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The Annapolis Valley, Gaspereau Valley, South Shore and Malagash Peninsula; grapes are also grown in places such as Cape Breton Island (Wikipedia)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: A small scale
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Area figures differ: about 1,000 acres (404 ha, Wine With Seth), 632 acres (256 ha) in 2015 (Wikipedia), about 400 ha (3% of Canada, as cited by Vins du Québec) and 530 ha (Wine With Seth's Canada page), so none is tested
slides.1.content: Nova Scotia's wine history is long but its industry is young.
slides.2.title: Climate and grapes
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Maritime moderation
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Atlantic moderates temperature extremes and extends the harvest window, and long autumns allow slow ripening; the growing season is just 5.5 months and minimum temperatures in favourable microclimates rarely drop below -23°C (Wine With Seth, Wikipedia); the Bay of Fundy also helps moderate winter temperatures (Wine With Seth's Canada page)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: L'Acadie Blanc
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The most important white, a hybrid suited to short, cool seasons, originally bred in Vineland, Ontario (Vineland 53261) and used for still and sparkling wines; other whites include Seyval Blanc, Vidal Blanc, Ortega and Geisenheim 318, with Riesling and Chardonnay in the warmest microclimates (Wine With Seth, Wikipedia)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Reds and hybrids
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Reds include Baco Noir, Maréchal Foch, Leon Millot and Luci Kuhlmann, plus Pinot Noir and Gamay; hybrids have traditionally dominated for their cold-hardiness and disease resistance, and wineries have recently tried vinifera with moderate success (Wine With Seth, Wikipedia)
slides.2.content: A maritime climate plus cold-hardy hybrids.
slides.3.title: Tidal Bay and sparkling wine
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Tidal Bay's rules
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Launched in June 2012 as Nova Scotia's first (and only) official appellation; wines must be 100% Nova Scotia-grown, no more than 11% alcohol, and approved each year by an independent blind tasting panel; the style is cool, crisp, lively and aromatic, with fresh green fruit, dynamic acidity and minerality (Wine Growers Nova Scotia)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Variety rules in detail
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Wikipedia says L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal and Geisenheim 318 must make up at least 51%, with 16 other varieties allowed; the official page shows the variety list only as an image that could not be checked, so the variety detail is not tested
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Traditional-method sparkling
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Nova Scotia is best known for sparkling wine: Benjamin Bridge, L'Acadie Vineyards and Blomidon Estate Winery use the traditional method and some bottles are sold outside the province; L'Acadie Vineyards' Prestige Brut Estate is made entirely from L'Acadie Blanc (Wikipedia, Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: Tidal Bay is a style standard, not just a grape list.
